Question_text: A student investigates how the resistance of a light-dependent resistor (LDR) depends on the brightness of light. He uses a lamp to vary the brightness of light on the LDR. The LDR is mounted on a wooden block so that it is a distance l above the bench. The lamp is placed directly above the LDR at a distance h above the bench, as shown in Fig. 1.1.
image: Fig. 1.1 is a diagram showing an experimental setup. A lamp is positioned above an LDR (light-dependent resistor), which is mounted on a wooden block resting on a bench. The vertical distance from the bench surface to the top of the wooden block (where the LDR sits) is labeled 'l'. The vertical distance from the bench surface to the lamp is labeled 'h'. A dashed line connects the lamp to the LDR, and the direct distance between them is labeled 'd'.

Parts.part_text: On Fig. 1.1, measure the distances l and h.
Calculate the distance d from the lamp to the LDR.
The student uses a ruler to measure h. Suggest one difficulty that the student has when making this measurement.
Fig. 1.2 shows some of the apparatus used in the experiment. In the space below, draw a circuit diagram for this apparatus.
Parts.image: Fig. 1.2 shows an apparatus diagram. It depicts an LDR, an ammeter with a scale of 0-100 mA, and a voltmeter with a scale of 0-10 V, connected with wires to a power supply (represented by '+' and '-' terminals). The LDR and ammeter appear to be in series, and the voltmeter is connected in parallel across the LDR.

Parts.part_text: Fig. 1.3 shows the readings of voltage V across the LDR and current I in the circuit when the lamp is at the distance d above the LDR calculated in (a)(ii). Record the readings V and I.
Parts.image: Fig. 1.3 displays two circular meter scales. The top meter, labeled 'V', shows a voltage reading of 6.0 V on a scale from 0 to 10. The bottom meter, labeled 'mA', shows a current reading of 50 mA on a scale from 0 to 100.

Parts.part_text: The resistance R of the LDR for this lamp position is calculated using the equation: R = V/I Calculate R, giving your answer to 2 significant figures with unit.

The student repeats the experiment for different values of d. The results are shown in Table 1.1. Use the readings taken in (a)(ii) and (b)(ii) to complete the top row of Table 1.1. On the grid in Fig. 1.4, plot the graph of I/mA on the y-axis against d/cm on the x-axis. Start your axes from (0,0). Draw the smooth curve of best fit.
Parts.image: Table 1.1 is provided with two columns, 'd/cm' and 'I/mA', showing experimental data points (e.g., 7.0 cm, 43 mA; 11.1 cm, 28 mA; 19.0 cm, 16 mA; 26.8 cm, 12 mA; 35.0 cm, 10 mA). Fig. 1.4 is a blank grid for plotting a graph, with axes originating from (0,0).

Parts.part_text: The voltage V is constant throughout. Suggest how the resistance R of the LDR varies with d.

Question_text: A student investigates the speed of sound v in air using an oscilloscope. He uses the apparatus shown in Fig. 2.1.
image: Fig. 2.1 is a diagram showing an experimental setup to measure the speed of sound. A student is holding a balloon and a pin, preparing to burst the balloon. Two microphones, labeled A and B, are placed in a straight line with the balloon. Both microphones are connected by wires to an oscilloscope.

Parts.part_text: The balloon and the two microphones are in a straight line. The student uses a pin to burst the balloon, creating a loud sound. The sound is detected first by the microphone at A and then by the microphone at B. The corresponding traces on the screen of the oscilloscope are shown in Fig. 2.2. The timebase on the oscilloscope is set to 0.50ms/division. Use Fig. 2.2 to calculate the time for the sound to travel from A to B.
Parts.image: Fig. 2.2 shows an oscilloscope screen displaying two wave traces. 'trace from microphone A' shows an initial spike at an earlier time. 'trace from microphone B' shows a similar spike at a later time. The horizontal separation between the start of the two spikes is 3.5 divisions. A horizontal arrow indicates the length of '1 division'.

Parts.part_text: The student uses an old metre rule to find the distance between A and B. Fig. 2.3 shows the position of A and of B on the metre rule, a distance of 82cm apart. Suggest a reason why the student did not place microphone A at the 0.0cm mark on this metre rule.
Parts.image: Fig. 2.3 shows a section of a metre rule marked from 10 cm to 90 cm. A vertical line labeled 'A' is positioned at the 10 cm mark, and another vertical line labeled 'B' is positioned at the 92 cm mark.

Parts.part_text: Use the equation V = distance travelled / time taken to calculate the speed v of sound.
Suggest one way in which the student can obtain a more accurate value for v using the same apparatus.

Question_text: A student investigates the upward force on a cylinder placed in water. He attaches the cylinder to the end of a newton meter before it is placed in water, as shown in Fig. 3.1.
image: Fig. 3.1 is a diagram showing a Newton meter suspended from a rod. A cylinder is attached to the bottom hook of the Newton meter and is partially submerged in water contained in a beaker. A magnified view of the Newton meter's scale is provided, clearly showing the pointer indicating a reading of 5.5 N.

Parts.part_text: State the weight of the cylinder before it is placed in water.
The student lowers the cylinder into the beaker of water until it is fully immersed. The new reading is shown in Fig. 3.2. State the new reading shown in Fig. 3.2.
Parts.image: Fig. 3.2 shows a magnified view of a Newton meter scale. The pointer is indicating a reading of 4.0 N.

Parts.part_text: Calculate the upward force on the cylinder due to the water.
The cylinder is shown in Fig. 3.3. The height h of the cylinder is 6.5cm and the diameter is 3.8 cm. Calculate the volume V of the cylinder using the equation: V = πd²h / 4
Parts.image: Fig. 3.3 is a diagram of a cylinder. Its height is labeled 'h', and its diameter across the top circular face is labeled 'd'.

Parts.part_text: The diameter d is measured with a ruler. Describe how this is done accurately. You may draw a diagram if you wish.

Theory suggests that the upward force on the cylinder is given by: upward force = Vgp where g = 10N/kg and ρ = 0.0010kg/cm³. Use your value of V from (c)(i) to calculate the upward force suggested by this theory.
State whether the value of the upward force determined in (b)(ii) supports the theory. Give a reason for your answer.

Question_text: A student does an investigation to find out whether cotton wool or bubble wrap is the better insulator. She is provided with the following apparatus: • a 100 cm³ glass beaker • a supply of hot water • a rectangular piece of cotton wool • a rectangular piece of bubble wrap • adhesive tape.
image: A diagram illustrating the provided apparatus: a glass beaker, a kettle representing 'hot water', a piece of cotton wool, and a piece of bubble wrap.

Parts.part_text: State two further pieces of apparatus that are needed for the investigation.
Describe in detail how the student does the investigation. State any measurements that need to be taken and explain how she decides which is the better insulator.
Explain how the student makes a fair comparison between the cotton wool and the bubble wrap.
